CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should prepare and announce targeted retaliatory tariffs on politically sensitive U.S. exports—particularly agricultural products (soybeans, sorghum) and coal—while publicly signaling willingness to negotiate. Retaliation should be calibrated to hit Trump's political base (farm states, coal country) to create domestic U.S. political pressure for de-escalation, while keeping the door open for talks.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.45 reflects that the U.S. is moving toward imposing up to $60 billion in tariffs on Chinese goods targeting technology, telecom, and apparel sectors, based on Section 301 findings (Yahoo Finance, reporting Trump rejected $30B for ~$60B). The U.S. is China's biggest export market, accounting for over 18% of total exports, and these tariffs could cause business collapse and job losses in export hubs. However, the threat is not yet existential: Brookings analysis notes that Chinese exports to the U.S. measured by value-added are only ~3% of GDP, and China's economy is transitioning toward consumption-based growth. The U.S. has also frozen formal trade dialogue mechanisms, signaling deteriorating diplomatic channels (Reuters).

The action score of -1.0 (retaliate) is justified because: (1) China's metals industry has already urged targeting U.S. coal, which is central to Trump's political base (Reuters); (2) Beijing has launched a sorghum probe signaling agricultural retaliation readiness (Reuters); (3) Brookings analysis confirms that Xi gains politically domestically by standing firm and that China has historically retaliated proportionately; (4) retaliation serves as deterrence—Beijing wants to demonstrate that challenging China yields more costs than benefits, discouraging other countries from following Washington's lead (Brookings); (5) the U.S. midterm elections in November 2018 create political pressure points that China can exploit, as Trump faces voters while Xi does not. Retaliation now, before the tariffs are formally imposed, signals resolve and may deter the full $60B package.
key_factors: U.S. Section 301 investigation leading to proposed ~$60B tariffs on Chinese tech, telecom, apparel
U.S. is China's largest export market (18%+ of total exports)
China's metals industry urging retaliation targeting U.S. coal sector
Sorghum probe launched by Beijing as retaliatory signal
Xi Jinping's domestic political incentive to stand firm against U.S. pressure
U.S. midterm elections in November 2018 creating asymmetric political pressure
U.S. has frozen formal trade dialogue mechanism with China
Chinese exports to U.S. measured by value-added only ~3% of GDP, limiting existential risk

sources_cited.excerpt: China's metals industry issued the country's most explicit threat yet in the row, urging on Friday for the government to retaliate by targeting U.S. coal

The dispute has fueled concerns that soybeans, the United States' most valuable export to the world's second largest economy, might be caught up in the trade actions after Beijing launched a probe into imports of U.S. sorghum
Xi gains politically in Beijing by standing firm against U.S. pressure and punching back against punitive measures. Historically, China has always retaliated proportionately to U.S. trade actions.
When measured by value added, Chinese exports to the United States account for only 3 percent of its GDP
Beijing also is determined to demonstrate that challenging China on trade issues yields more costs than benefits

Xi likely calculates that Trump needs Xi more (on North Korea) than vice versa. Beijing believes any trade war would hurt the U.S. economy, which would have a more immediate political effect in the United States than China. Xi will not face a referendum on his performance any time soon, whereas the United States has its midterm elections this November
Trump has rejected a tariff proposal worth $30 billion on Chinese imports for a much steeper figure of almost $60 billion
The United States is China's biggest export market, accounting for more than 18% of total export
the United States has frozen a formal mechanism for talks on commercial disputes with China because it is not satisfied Beijing has met its promises to ease market restrictions
